To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified 23 mutations in ACVRL (ALK1) and 8 in endoglin (ENG), including a novel duplication of exons (4 to 8) and 2 deletions (exon 1 to 2 and 9 to14), which increase the mutation rate of the 2 genes to 88% in French HHT families.
the mutation rate of ENG and ACVL1 genes is high (88%) in French HHT families, and that ACVRL1 mutations are more frequent than ENG mutations.
the mutation rate in French patients with HHT is 88% and that ENG mutations are more likely to result in large insertions/deletion and to be associated to a milder phenotype.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of mutations in HHT patients, and the characterization of the molecular pathology in HERT, and has led to a better understanding of the disease.
the characterization of the mutations of two major genes in French HHT.
the identification of the genetic basis of HHT and provides the first molecular characterization of the largest cohort of French HHT patients.

88% of HHT patients have mutations of either ENG or ACVRI.
mutations of ENG and/or ACVRL1 are found in 88% of the French patients with HHT.
mutations of ACVRL (80.1%) are more frequent than ENG mutations (9.6%) in HHT patients, with a prevalence of 10.2% of large rearrangements in the ENG gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
88% of HHT patients with a confirmed diagnosis of HHT have a mutation in one of the two major genes.
the ENG gene is mutated in 8% (8/119) of HHT patients and the ACVRL1 gene is mutated in the remaining 90% (111/119) of patients.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the molecular diagnosis of HHT should include the search for large mutations in ENG and ACVLR1, in addition to the sequencing of the coding sequences.
